## My Thinking

I have farmed this land in Quzhou my whole life. My father farmed it, I farmed it, and I know what works here. At 65, my back is not what it used to be, and my son has moved to work in the city. I cannot afford to experiment or take risks — I need steady grain income and something I can mostly manage with hired help at the busy times.

The land here is flat, the wells are deep, and the soil is good loam. Everyone around me grows winter wheat followed by summer maize. This rotation has fed my family for generations and I have no reason to change it now.

I have about 8 mu of contracted land. All of it goes into wheat-maize. I would never split it into specialty crops — I don't know those markets and I'm too old to learn a new crop.

For wheat, I'll do rotary tillage after the maize harvest in October, then sow an improved variety like 矮抗58 — I've used it for years, it stands well and doesn't lodge. I spread compound fertilizer as base and top-dress urea at jointing. I'll water four times: the winter freeze-in water, green-up, jointing, and grain-fill. I'll spray once for aphids and once for powdery mildew in spring.

For maize, I'll machine-plant right after wheat harvest, no-till, straight into the stubble — saves my back and the county extension station has been pushing this for years. I buy whatever hybrid seeds the local supply cooperative recommends, usually Zhengdan 958 or similar. Summer rains are usually enough but I'll run the pump once if July is dry.

My fertilizer rates follow local habit and what the county extension station recommends — moderate nitrogen, some phosphorus and potassium applied as compound base fertilizer plus a urea top-dress. Wheat needs four irrigations from my deep well given the dry climate here; maize mostly relies on summer rain with one backup pump run if needed. I use rotary tillage for wheat to bury maize residue, then switch to no-till direct seeding for maize to reduce labour.
